sections.text: 2.3.1 Preparation of Film Materials To ensure film flexibility, glycerol was added as a plasticizer to the film‐forming solution to keep water molecules within polymer; the resulting matrix is known as thermoplastic starch (TPS) (Agarwal  2021 ). First, the amount of glycerol was determined on the basis of preliminary studies conducted without incorporation of nanofiller in structure. Starch was first dried in oven at 70°C for approximately 12 h to remove free water (Aouada et al.  2011 ). Glycerol was added to starch at varying dry weight ratios (30%, 40%, 50%, and 60% w/w, based on starch) and dissolved by mixing in water using a magnetic stirrer with a heating plate. Then, the mixture was poured into a Petri dish and dried at 30°C ± 2°C for 15 h. The quantity of plasticizer has a significant impact on macroscopic properties of starch‐based films (Agarwal  2021 ). The film material containing 40% glycerol ensured good processability and formation of uniform structure, with this concentration yielding the most favorable results in terms of overall appearance, exhibiting desirable macroscopic characteristics, such as smoothness, non‐brittleness, rigidity, sturdiness, flexibility, non‐sticky surface upon handling, and ease of detachment from the Petri dish. Starch nanocomposite films were subsequently produced by solvent casting method, as shown in Figure  2 . The preparation procedure for biocomposite materials was modified on the basis of techniques outlined by Aouada et al. ( 2011 ) and Suryanto et al. ( 2019 ). Dried starch (5.0% w/v, based on final volume of solution) and glycerol (40% w/w, based on starch) were weighed and mixed with 50 mL of ultrapure water. The mixture was stirred using a magnetic stirrer for 1 h at room temperature (Mixture A). Clay concentration in the matrix was studied at levels of 3% and 5% (w/w, based on starch). A known quantity of organoclay and surfactant‐free clay was weighed, and 50 mL of ultrapure water was added (Mixture B). Mixture B was stirred for 16 h at room temperature on a magnetic stirrer, then ultrasonic treatment (35 kHz, 860 W, 60 min) was performed in an ultrasonic bath (Sonorex RK514BH, BANDELIN Electronic GmbH & Co. KG, Berlin, Germany) to prevent agglomeration of clay in the biocomposite material and to ensure homogeneous distribution. Mixtures A and B were then combined and stirred for 1 h at room temperature. As control film (S), starch and glycerol were weighed, and 100 mL of ultrapure water was put in without adding clay/organoclay, followed by stirring for 2 h. After stirring for 20 min at gelatinization temperature (65–70°C), 25 mL of film‐forming solution was cast onto Petri dishes (90 × 17 mm 2 ) and allowed to dry at 30°C ± 2°C for 24 h in oven. The dried films were removed from Petri dishes and kept in a desiccator until measurements were conducted. The thickness of film materials was 0.187 ± 0.017 mm. 1 Introduction Packaging industry has utilized nanoparticles to improve polymer properties, particularly layered inorganic materials such as clays, due to availability, cost‐effectiveness, substantial performance enhancements, and easy processing. Nanoscale fillers can encompass a variety of nanomaterials, including nanoclay, and are tailored for specific applications. Well‐delaminated and exfoliated nanoclay layers within polymer structure can serve as barriers by increasing the tortuosity of diffusion pathways for penetrants (Echegoyen et al.  2016 ; Nasiri et al.  2016 ; Kumari et al.  2024 ). Montmorillonite (Mt, MMT) is hydrated alumina‐silicate clay phyllosilicate with an octahedral aluminum hydroxide layer sandwiched between two silica tetrahedral layers (Chai et al.  2024 ). It is extensively used across different fields owing to its high specific surface area, cation exchange capacity, platelet aspect ratio, swelling ability, and convenience of surface modification (Mahesh et al.  2011 ; Nasiri et al.  2016 ). Nevertheless, narrow clay layer spacing hinders diffusion of polymer chains into galleries, causing clay particle aggregation, which can be overcome by modifying clay surfaces with surfactant molecules to replace exchangeable inorganic ions, facilitating intercalation and exfoliation of clay layers, increasing basal space, and yielding organomodified MMT (oMt) (Mahesh et al.  2011 ; Törnük  2014 ). Starch, a granular polysaccharide composed of highly branched amylopectin and predominantly linear amylose, is a potential food packaging biopolymer based on its abundance, low cost, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and outstanding film‐forming characteristics. However, hydrophilicity is a challenge for starch‐based materials due to free hydroxyl groups. Hydrophobicity can be obtained by replacing hydrophilic groups with hydrophobic ones, such as embedding clay nanofillers into a matrix (Agarwal  2021 ). In recent years, polymer nanocomposites have attracted considerable attention in materials science due to their wide application potential (Bai et al.  2020 ). Numerous studies have explored the incorporation of clay nanofillers in polymers. For instance, Alboofetileh et al. ( 2013 ) studied sodium alginate‐based nanocomposites containing Mtand reported that the addition of Mt increased water resistance, reduced permeability of water vapor, decreased elongation, and improved tensile strength of nanocomposites. Mansour et al. ( 2020 ) studied effects of unmodified and modified Mt in maize starch biocomposites and obtained improvements in morphological, mechanical, and optical properties. Similarly, Bai et al. ( 2020 ) synthesized hydrophobic polyacrylamide–Mt nanocomposites with improved viscoelasticity, thermal stability, and shear resistance. Studies in the literature on Mt clay have mainly focused on mechanical, thermal, permeability, and optical properties, whereas uncertainties remain regarding the effect of clay/organoclay incorporation on the migration of substances from nanocomposite materials to food/food simulants. This research aimed to investigate the effects of cationic and non‐ionic surfactants on the modification of Mt to increase its basal spacing. Particle size analysis, zeta potential, electrical conductivity, Fourier transform infrared (FT‐IR), and X‐ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were conducted to examine the effect of organomodification. Organoclays that exhibited the best characterization results were incorporated into a starch matrix to manufacture bio‐based nanocomposite food packaging films, the water absorption capacity and water solubility of which were analyzed. Overall and specific migration rates of nanocomposites into aqueous and acidic simulants were assessed, considering potential food safety concerns. The significance of the present study lies in the development of starch–organoclay film materials and investigation of their potential use as food packaging materials based on migration properties, in compliance with regulations in the European Union (EU) and Türkiye.

The migration analyses were conducted on the basis of the total immersion method. 2.3.3.1 Overall Migration Analysis Addition of organoclay into starch polymer was evaluated for aqueous and acidic food simulants. ( 2020 ) studied the stability of organoclay emulsions containing non‐ionic surfactant (Tween 20) by investigating the changes in the mean particle diameter of emulsion. When the ratio of surfactant was increased, the synergy between Tween 20 and Mt was enhanced. Tween 20 facilitated flocculation of solid particles at water–oil interface, creating a space barrier that inhibited fusion of emulsion droplets, collision, and aggregation. This process resulted in a reduction of the average particle diameter of emulsion. Nevertheless, further increases in surfactant ratio in organoclay led to an increase in average particle size of emulsion to varying degrees. As the concentration of solid particles increased, surfactant molecules facilitated greater adsorption of particles at the interface of water and oil, resulting in the formation of double or multilayer structures. This phenomenon contributed to the enlargement of mean particle diameter of emulsion. Similarly, in our study, decrease in particle size (<500 nm) occurred with the addition of non‐ionic surfactant to clay. However, when the amount of surfactant was increased to 4‐Tween‐oMt level, the mean particle diameter of emulsion enlarged to 690.7 nm. As a result, mean particle diameters for emulsion stabilized by 3‐Tween‐oMt exhibited the smallest particle size (425.5 nm) for the non‐ionic surfactant. In our study, no linear increase in mean particle size was observed as a result of increasing surfactant level for both types of surfactants. Similar results were obtained by Yang et al. ( 2020 ) when studying different non‐ionic Tween surfactants (Tween20, 40, 60, 80, 85). Hydrophobic chain tail lengthens from Tween 20 to Tween 85, whereas the mean particle diameters for emulsions stabilized by Tween20 (337.1 nm), Tween40 (401.6 nm), Tween60 (342.5 nm), Tween80 (413.1 nm), and Tween85 (314.3 nm). So, they performed interfacial tension tests to explain why the mean particle diameter of stabilized emulsion did not increase smoothly. The addition of surfactant resulted in a substantial decrease in interfacial tension of emulsion, showing the synergy between Mt clay and surfactant. The use of surfactants altered wetting properties, caused particle size flocculation, and enhanced suspension stability. The surfactant adsorbed at particle interface on the surface of droplets, thereby decreasing interfacial tension and resulting in smaller particle sizes. Delamination of Mt clay is characterized by reduction in particle size and increase in specific surface area. The extent of delamination is influenced by the swelling capacity of clay (Mahmoodi et al.  2019 ). Mahmoodi et al. ( 2019 ) investigated the adsorption behavior of cationic surfactants onto Mt. As cationic surfactant concentration increased, the particle size of Mt increased, explained by the intercalation of positive tails of cationic surfactants in the internal layers of Mt for this phenomenon. Because of the complexity of colloidal systems, aggregation phenomena can be challenging. Brownian motion, which is random movement of particles inside suspension, causes colloidal particles to undergo unstable movement as a result of collisions with molecules of solvent and particles. This kinetic behavior can cause particle collisions followed by aggregation, thereby complicating precise regulation of cluster dimensions. Electrostatic interactions can also be another critical factor in colloidal systems, capable of triggering interactions that facilitate particle aggregation. It can be challenging to control these interactions, particularly in complex solutions, where they are modulated by factors such as particle dimensions, morphology of particles, ionic strength, dynamic interactions, and pH. Additionally, colloidal particles are influenced by van der Waals interactions in solution (Rodriguez‐Loya et al.  2024 ). When surfactant is included, adsorption of surfactant molecules onto clay interlayers may change zeta potential, increase electrostatic repulsion between platelets, and consequently lead to particle size reduction. This situation affects both van der Waals interactions and electrostatic repulsion. As surfactant concentration continues to increase, adsorption of surfactant molecules finally reaches a saturation point. Excess surfactant may then cause hydrophobic interactions, leading to micelle formation, which can cause an increase in particle size despite zeta potential remaining positive/negative (Mahmoodi et al.  2019 ; Moslemizadeh et al.  2016 ; Rodriguez‐Loya et al.  2024 ). Nanoemulsion systems are thermodynamically unstable and characterized by particle sizes typically smaller than 500 nm. The size of the particles in nanoemulsion is significantly influenced by the amount of surfactant added (Yang et al.  2020 ). In the evaluation of the type and amount of surfactant in Mt clay, it will be important to assess characterization analyses collectively and in conjunction with other characterization methods. On the basis of data presented in Table  2 , the delamination and swelling of organoclay solutions below 6‐CTAB‐oMt (361.3 nm) and 3‐Tween‐oMt (425.5 nm) levels were considered to be the factors contributing to low average particle size (<500 nm) within the aqueous phase of applied surfactants. The obtained organoclays had good suspension stability and slow agglomeration in aqueous colloidal media up to 6‐CTAB‐oMt level for cationic surfactant and 3‐Tween‐oMt level for non‐ionic surfactant, both of which had low average particle size (<500 nm) (Törnük  2014 ; Yang et al.  2020 ). 3.1.2 Zeta Potential As shown in Figure  3 , the zeta potential value of blank clay (Mt) was measured as negative (−27.0 mV), which was consistent with the negatively charged surface of Mt (Karaca et al.  2013 ). With increasing concentrations of cationic surfactant, negative zeta potential values gradually decreased and approached zero, after that shifting to positive values (ranging from +11.9 to +38.5 mV). This trend can be explained by the screening effect on electrical charges of Mt surface and electrostatic interactions, which led to a decrease in the magnitude of zeta potential. This change occurred due to electrostatic interactions between positive ions (CTA + ) in surfactant and negative regions on the surface of Mt (Güngör et al.  2001 ). Transition of zeta potential values from negative to positive signified a shift in the orientation of positive ions from parallel structure (monolayer or bilayers) to perpendicular arrangement (pseudo‐trilayers or paraffin‐type layers) at interface (Karaca et al.  2013 ). The magnitude of zeta potential serves as an indicator of potential stability of a colloidal system. When all particles in a suspension exhibit notably high negative/positive zeta potential, they tend to repel each other, thereby minimizing the possibility of flocculation. In contrast, if particles have low values of zeta potential, there is insufficient force to prevent them from flocculating/aggregating. The threshold that typically distinguishes stable from unstable suspensions is set at approximately ±30 mV. The particles with zeta potential falling below −30 mV and exceeding +30 mV are generally regarded as stable (Malvern  2013 ). In our study, the stability was obtained at 5‐CTAB‐oMt and higher concentrations of CTAB surfactant, based on zeta potential, indicating that nanoparticles were quite stable. One of the primary factors influencing zeta potential is pH (Malvern  2013 ). Because the surface charge of nanoparticles depends on the pH of the solution, zeta potential changes with the pH value of the medium in which particles are located (Ateş  2018 ). In this study, the pH of solutions was similar and close to neutral (7.710 ± 0.133). As shown in Figure  4 , the zeta potential value of organoclay decreased from −27.0 to −21.0 mV as a result of the addition of non‐ionic surfactant. This reduction suggests that non‐ionic Tween80 might have caused a less stable structure. The decreased surface potential may indicate weaker repulsion between colloidal particles and higher aggregation kinetics (Törnük  2014 ). It can be said that among the tested concentrations, 3‐Tween‐oMt level (−23.5 mV) was the closest to −30 mV stability threshold. The decreasing behavior of zeta potential in non‐ionic surfactant‐modified Mt dispersions, compared to blank dispersion, was likely resulting from the relocation of ionic species at oil/water boundary. As indicated in the study by Roldan‐Cruz et al. ( 2016 ), the characteristics of surface charges at water–oil interface are not unclear. The interfacial charge can result from the imbalance of ions present at the surface, which are produced by hydroxide (OH − ) and hydrogen (H + ) ions in water molecules. Moreover, the ions generated by dissolved carbon dioxide (CO 3 
 2−  and HCO 3 
 − ) could potentially cause an additional impact. The adsorption of non‐ionic surfactant molecules may cause relocation of ionic species from interface, thus suppressing interface charge and reducing zeta potential. Ion concentration correlates with solution conductivity, and a breakpoint in the conductivity graph indicates CMC of surfactant, where micelle formation occurs (Bhattarai et al.  2015 ). Surfactants have ability to spontaneously organize into a variety of micellar formations above CMC. The concentration range is limited to values below or close to CMC, where adsorption reaches its peak for ionic surfactants in organoclay preparation (Guégan  2019 ). In diluted ionic surfactant solutions, conductivity generally increases linearly with concentration. Beyond CMC point, the ratios of different ions (such as micelles, monomers, and counterions) change, resulting in a different slope for specific conductivity in relation to concentration. CMC can be identified by analyzing two straight lines intersecting on a conductivity versus concentration graph, specifically at the point where the slope changes. At elevated surfactant concentrations, the interactions among charged species generally lead to a reduction in ionic mobilities. Consequently, conductivity no longer exhibits a linear relationship with concentration (Durand‐Vidal et al.  2020 ). In our study for cationic surfactant‐modified organoclay, 5‐CTAB‐oMt was determined as CMC point. As indicated, the conductivity is related to ion concentration in solution. FT‐IR serves as an effective method for analyzing functional groups (Mahesh et al.  2011 ). With the addition of ionic and non‐ionic surfactants to clay, the appearance of asymmetric methylene (CH 2 ) stretching, symmetric CH 2  stretching, and CH 2  bending vibration peaks showed that alkyl groups of surfactants were located in clay interlayers. When cationic surfactant content in organoclay increased, new bands were observed in the range of 2927–2918, 2855–2849, 1488–1486, and 792–786 cm −1 , which related to vibrations of asymmetric CH 2  stretching, symmetric CH 2  stretching, CH 2  scissoring bending, and CH 2  rocking bending, respectively. Typically, the intensity of these new peaks increased with higher surfactant concentrations, suggesting that a greater amount of surfactant is intercalating into clay (Chanra et al.  2019 ). Kung and Hayes ( 1993 ) also pointed out that relative shifts in vibrational modes of CH 2  can be used in the evaluation of hydrophobic properties of surfactant added. Accordingly, lower frequency (energy) values reflect a more hydrophobic structure. The results obtained in this work showed that the degree of hydrophobic properties could increase with higher surfactant loading. In Table  5 , the wavelengths (energies) of CH 2  asymmetric stretching, symmetric stretching, and bending (scissoring and rocking) vibration peaks decreased with an increase in the concentration of cationic surfactant that adsorbed on clay. At relatively high surfactant levels, most of the hydration cations were surrounded by surfactant cations, which reduced the amount of water to be adsorbed, causing surface properties to change from hydrophilic to hydrophobic (Karaca et al.  2013 ). When cationic surfactant was intercalated into clay interfacial galleries, changes were also observed in Si─O─Si stretching and bending vibrations within the tetrahedral structure. Si─O─Si stretching vibration was detected at 987 cm −1  for unmodified Mt and increased to 996 cm −1  with CTAB addition, then decreased to 991 cm −1  with further surfactant increase. Si─O─Si bending vibration band was observed at 415 cm −1  for unmodified Mt and increased to 431 cm −1  with the addition of surfactant. Accordingly, the change in Si─O─Si stretching band indicated interaction between surfactant molecules and siloxane (Si─O) clay surface. The change in Si─O vibration band proved that interaction/bonding between the surfactant and silicate surface increased (Xi et al.  2005 ). Generally, it was determined that after the levels of 4‐CTAB‐oMt and 5‐CTAB‐oMt, wavelengths of absorption bands either remained the same or decreased. The FT‐IR spectrum of Mt treated with different concentrations of non‐ionic Tween80 surfactant showed intense absorption peaks of functional groups in the structure. With the increase of Tween80 concentration, new bands were observed in the range of 2930–2925, 2855–2852, 1463–1460, and 791–787 cm −1 , which correspond to vibrations of asymmetric CH 2  stretching, symmetric CH 2  stretching, CH 2  scissoring bending, and CH 2  rocking bending, respectively. These new peaks were more pronounced, especially in 3‐Tween‐oMt and 4‐Tween‐oMt spectra. It was also expected that C═O stretching vibration peak, belonging to ester group, would appear in the range of 1735–1725 cm −1  (Kura et al.  2014 ). Although C═O vibration band was absent in 1‐Tween‐oMt and 2‐Tween‐oMt, it appeared at 1725 and 1732 cm −1  in 3‐Tween‐oMt and 4‐Tween‐oMt, respectively, with increased surfactant concentration. They calculated the layer spacing as 1.24 nm for Na–Mt and 2.15 nm for oMt. In our study, the increase in  d ‐spacing and the decrease in 2 θ  value showed separation between clay platelets and effective diffusion of surfactant molecules into layered silicate (Zawrah et al.  2014 ). Therefore, at specified surfactant levels, organomodification process was successfully carried out, and layer gaps of modified Mt considerably increased. For alkylammonium cationic surfactants, organoclay is obtained by intercalation of surfactant molecules through ion exchange with inorganic cations located in interlayer regions of clay. This process changes characteristics of Mt clay from hydrophilic to hydrophobic (Guégan  2019 ). The alkylammonium ions can form different interlamellar arrangements, which are monolayer, bilayers, pseudo‐trilayers, and paraffin‐type layer configurations, depending on the concentration of cationic surfactant, which affects basal spacing. Monolayer configuration has 13.6 Å (1.36 nm) typical basal spacing, and surfactant chains are arranged parallel to silicate layers. For bilayer structure, basal spacing is 17.6 Å, and two alkyl chains are arranged parallel to silicate layers. In pseudo‐trilayer arrangement, polar end groups of surfactant chains attach to silicate layers. Therefore, unpolar end groups of alkylammonium ions are shifted one above the other, and the thickness of three alkyl chains determines interlayer separation, yielding basal spacing of approximately 22 Å. For paraffin‐type layers, chains in all trans conformation point away from surface, whereas ammonium groups remain bonded to silicate layer, and basal spacing increases (>22 Å) depending on the number of various methyl end group orientations (Zawrah et al.  2014 ). Karaca et al. ( 2013 ) investigated the zeta potential of organoclays obtained by adding different amounts of CTAB surfactant to Mt. Negative zeta potential value of unmodified Mt increased to positive values with CTAB surfactant, which was explained by the orientation change of CTA +  ions in the basal space of clay layers from horizontal (monolayer or bilayers) to vertical positions (pseudo‐trilayers or paraffin‐type layers) (Karaca et al.  2013 ). In our study, 5‐CTAB‐oMt organoclay exhibited a zeta potential of +30.5 mV, which corresponded to basal spacing characteristic of pseudo‐trilayer structure (<22 Å), indicating successful intercalation of cationic surfactant between clay layers. The adsorption of amphiphilic surfactants in Mt clay differs from electrostatic interactions or ion exchange exhibited by cationic surfactants. The main force for adsorption between clay and non‐ionic surfactant is ion–dipole interactions. In the absence of positive charge and hydrogen bonds in interlayers for non‐ionic surfactants, ion–dipole interactions primarily control adsorption. This ensures that exchangeable inorganic cations are preserved after adsorption in clay structure, which provides both hydrophobic and hydrophilic behavior of organoclay. In general, non‐ionic surfactants adsorb on clay surfaces as lateral monolayer or bilayer structures, with interlayer spacing limited to 1.2–1.8 nm (12–18 Å) (Guégan  2019 ). Kang and Jeong ( 2015 ) studied the sorption of non‐ionic surfactant Tween80 by soil minerals. They investigated XRD patterns of Mt clay that had reacted with Tween80 surfactant. The  d ‐spacing of non‐ionic surfactant‐modified Mt clay increased to 16.5–18.9 from 12.6 Å, which was associated with the basal spacing of unmodified Mt. The  d 
 001  value of Mt increased with the addition of Tween80, indicating that absorption of Tween80 between layers results in expansion. In our study,  d ‐spacing value (16.1 Å) obtained for 3‐Tween‐oMt organoclay was consistent with the literature. Literature shows that adding nanoclay up to a certain level in materials can reduce total migration, as found in this work. In the study undertaken by Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ), the production of biodegradable nanocomposite films was obtained by incorporating varying concentrations (0.25%–0.50%–1%–3%–5% w/w) of HNT nanoclay into ST/PVA/GL matrix. Relevant studies in the literature, as demonstrated in the present study, indicate that incorporating nanoclay into material leads to specific migration of aluminum. In the study conducted by Farhoodi et al. ( 2014 ), nanocomposite samples were prepared by blending commercial organoclay into polyethylene terephthalate matrix. Total immersion method using 3% acetic acid was employed to evaluate specific migration of Al element at 25°C and 45°C for 7–90 days. The portions of simulants were taken at time intervals, and aluminum concentration was analyzed. The results indicated that specific migration of Al increased with prolonged storage time and higher temperature. At 25°C, aluminum levels rose from 0.03 mg/kg on Day 10 to 0.18 mg/kg on Day 90, whereas at 45°C, migration increased from 0.06 to 0.34 mg/kg over the same period. Specific migration results obtained in our study using acidic simulant were generally lower compared to the findings reported by Farhoodi et al. ( 2014 ). Although the main polymer matrices examined in two studies differ, this discrepancy may be attributed to the shorter contact time employed in our study. Mauricio‐Iglesias et al. ( 2010 ) incorporated Mt into wheat gluten matrix to develop food contact materials and investigated migration properties in water, 3% acetic acid, and 15% ethanol simulants after 10 days of storage at 40°C. Their results indicated that significant amounts of Al migration were detected only in acidic simulant, as observed in our study. This was attributed to the greater solubility of Al under low pH conditions, as Mt can undergo ion exchange within its interlayer regions. In the presence of acetic acid, an abundance of hydrogen ions may have replaced some of interlayer aluminum ions, which could explain aluminum migration. As stated by Council of Europe ( 1992 ), 3% acetic acid is regarded as the most aggressive simulant in terms of metal migration for plastics. Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ) investigated specific migration of Al ions from halloysite nanoclay combined into developed ST/PVA/GL biomaterial at 40°C for 10 days, using acidic and aqueous simulants. Aluminum ions were detected in both simulants; however, in contrast to the findings of our study, they reported higher migration levels in the aqueous simulant compared to the acidic one. This outcome was attributed to the hydrophilic character of 10% ethanol, which exhibited a solvent‐like effect on nanocomposites similar to that of water. This interaction enhanced the mobility of polymer chains, thereby facilitating the release of nanoclay from matrix. Additionally, it was reported that increasing HNT content in matrix led to a rise in Al migration for both simulants. In our study, a similar trend was observed by increasing the cationic surfactant‐modified organoclay ratio from 3% to 5% in matrix. This phenomenon was attributed to the formation of nanoclay agglomerates at higher nanoparticle concentrations, leading to poor interfacial bonding and greater migration into acidic simulant compared to well‐dispersed nanoparticles embedded in polymer matrix (Abdullah and Dong  2019 ). In food simulants, two mechanisms influence the mass transfer of nanoparticles: embedding (intermolecular interactions between polymer chains and penetrants) and diffusion, known as dual sorption theory. Among these, the diffusion proceeds at a faster rate than the embedding mechanism. Acetic acid and water molecules first embed in the matrix, then act as plasticizers, expanding polymer chains. This expansion causes the migration of nanoparticles through the equilibrated matrix (Farhoodi et al.  2014 ; Abdullah and Dong  2019 ; Huang et al.  2011 ). However, the primary advantage of incorporating nanoclay lies in its ability to significantly increase barrier properties of material against the permeation of gases or liquids (penetrants). The most widely accepted explanation for the improvement in barrier properties is provided by Nielsen's theory (Nielsen  1967 ). According to this theory, when nanofillers like clay in matrix are impermeable to liquid or gas molecules, these penetrant molecules are forced to navigate around fillers, resulting in a tortuous diffusion path (Mahesh et al.  2011 ; Törnük  2014 ). This increased diffusion path length effectively prolongs migration route and improves the barrier efficiency of the material. Due to the relatively rapid nature of the diffusion mechanism compared to the slower embedding process, diffusion of acetic acid molecules into starch‐based nanocomposites contributed to expansion between polymeric chains and promoted release of clay/organoclay. Therefore, it can be stated that in our study, the diffusion mechanism played a dominant role in controlling specific migration rates, which were higher in acidic simulant compared to hydrophilic counterparts.

Delamination of Mt clay is characterized by reduction in particle size and increase in specific surface area. The extent of delamination is influenced by the swelling capacity of clay (Mahmoodi et al.  2019 ). Mahmoodi et al. ( 2019 ) investigated the adsorption behavior of cationic surfactants onto Mt. As cationic surfactant concentration increased, the particle size of Mt increased, explained by the intercalation of positive tails of cationic surfactants in the internal layers of Mt for this phenomenon. Because of the complexity of colloidal systems, aggregation phenomena can be challenging. Brownian motion, which is random movement of particles inside suspension, causes colloidal particles to undergo unstable movement as a result of collisions with molecules of solvent and particles. This kinetic behavior can cause particle collisions followed by aggregation, thereby complicating precise regulation of cluster dimensions. Electrostatic interactions can also be another critical factor in colloidal systems, capable of triggering interactions that facilitate particle aggregation. It can be challenging to control these interactions, particularly in complex solutions, where they are modulated by factors such as particle dimensions, morphology of particles, ionic strength, dynamic interactions, and pH. Additionally, colloidal particles are influenced by van der Waals interactions in solution (Rodriguez‐Loya et al.  2024 ). When surfactant is included, adsorption of surfactant molecules onto clay interlayers may change zeta potential, increase electrostatic repulsion between platelets, and consequently lead to particle size reduction. This situation affects both van der Waals interactions and electrostatic repulsion. As surfactant concentration continues to increase, adsorption of surfactant molecules finally reaches a saturation point. Excess surfactant may then cause hydrophobic interactions, leading to micelle formation, which can cause an increase in particle size despite zeta potential remaining positive/negative (Mahmoodi et al.  2019 ; Moslemizadeh et al.  2016 ; Rodriguez‐Loya et al.  2024 ). Nanoemulsion systems are thermodynamically unstable and characterized by particle sizes typically smaller than 500 nm. The size of the particles in nanoemulsion is significantly influenced by the amount of surfactant added (Yang et al.  2020 ). In the evaluation of the type and amount of surfactant in Mt clay, it will be important to assess characterization analyses collectively and in conjunction with other characterization methods. The obtained organoclays had good suspension stability and slow agglomeration in aqueous colloidal media up to 6‐CTAB‐oMt level for cationic surfactant and 3‐Tween‐oMt level for non‐ionic surfactant, both of which had low average particle size (<500 nm) (Törnük  2014 ; Yang et al.  2020 ). 3.1.2 Zeta Potential As shown in Figure  3 , the zeta potential value of blank clay (Mt) was measured as negative (−27.0 mV), which was consistent with the negatively charged surface of Mt (Karaca et al.  2013 ). With increasing concentrations of cationic surfactant, negative zeta potential values gradually decreased and approached zero, after that shifting to positive values (ranging from +11.9 to +38.5 mV). This trend can be explained by the screening effect on electrical charges of Mt surface and electrostatic interactions, which led to a decrease in the magnitude of zeta potential. This change occurred due to electrostatic interactions between positive ions (CTA + ) in surfactant and negative regions on the surface of Mt (Güngör et al.  2001 ). Transition of zeta potential values from negative to positive signified a shift in the orientation of positive ions from parallel structure (monolayer or bilayers) to perpendicular arrangement (pseudo‐trilayers or paraffin‐type layers) at interface (Karaca et al.  2013 ). The magnitude of zeta potential serves as an indicator of potential stability of a colloidal system. When all particles in a suspension exhibit notably high negative/positive zeta potential, they tend to repel each other, thereby minimizing the possibility of flocculation. In contrast, if particles have low values of zeta potential, there is insufficient force to prevent them from flocculating/aggregating. The threshold that typically distinguishes stable from unstable suspensions is set at approximately ±30 mV. The particles with zeta potential falling below −30 mV and exceeding +30 mV are generally regarded as stable (Malvern  2013 ). In our study, the stability was obtained at 5‐CTAB‐oMt and higher concentrations of CTAB surfactant, based on zeta potential, indicating that nanoparticles were quite stable. One of the primary factors influencing zeta potential is pH (Malvern  2013 ). Because the surface charge of nanoparticles depends on the pH of the solution, zeta potential changes with the pH value of the medium in which particles are located (Ateş  2018 ). In this study, the pH of solutions was similar and close to neutral (7.710 ± 0.133). As shown in Figure  4 , the zeta potential value of organoclay decreased from −27.0 to −21.0 mV as a result of the addition of non‐ionic surfactant. This reduction suggests that non‐ionic Tween80 might have caused a less stable structure. The decreased surface potential may indicate weaker repulsion between colloidal particles and higher aggregation kinetics (Törnük  2014 ). It can be said that among the tested concentrations, 3‐Tween‐oMt level (−23.5 mV) was the closest to −30 mV stability threshold. The decreasing behavior of zeta potential in non‐ionic surfactant‐modified Mt dispersions, compared to blank dispersion, was likely resulting from the relocation of ionic species at oil/water boundary. As indicated in the study by Roldan‐Cruz et al. ( 2016 ), the characteristics of surface charges at water–oil interface are not unclear. The interfacial charge can result from the imbalance of ions present at the surface, which are produced by hydroxide (OH − ) and hydrogen (H + ) ions in water molecules. The adsorption of non‐ionic surfactant molecules may cause relocation of ionic species from interface, thus suppressing interface charge and reducing zeta potential. With the addition of ionic and non‐ionic surfactants to clay, the appearance of asymmetric methylene (CH 2 ) stretching, symmetric CH 2  stretching, and CH 2  bending vibration peaks showed that alkyl groups of surfactants were located in clay interlayers. Typically, the intensity of these new peaks increased with higher surfactant concentrations, suggesting that a greater amount of surfactant is intercalating into clay (Chanra et al.  2019 ). Kung and Hayes ( 1993 ) also pointed out that relative shifts in vibrational modes of CH 2  can be used in the evaluation of hydrophobic properties of surfactant added. Accordingly, lower frequency (energy) values reflect a more hydrophobic structure. The results obtained in this work showed that the degree of hydrophobic properties could increase with higher surfactant loading. In Table  5 , the wavelengths (energies) of CH 2  asymmetric stretching, symmetric stretching, and bending (scissoring and rocking) vibration peaks decreased with an increase in the concentration of cationic surfactant that adsorbed on clay. Si─O─Si bending vibration band was observed at 415 cm −1  for unmodified Mt and increased to 431 cm −1  with the addition of surfactant. Accordingly, the change in Si─O─Si stretching band indicated interaction between surfactant molecules and siloxane (Si─O) clay surface. The change in Si─O vibration band proved that interaction/bonding between the surfactant and silicate surface increased (Xi et al.  2005 ). Generally, it was determined that after the levels of 4‐CTAB‐oMt and 5‐CTAB‐oMt, wavelengths of absorption bands either remained the same or decreased. They calculated the layer spacing as 1.24 nm for Na–Mt and 2.15 nm for oMt. In our study, the increase in  d ‐spacing and the decrease in 2 θ  value showed separation between clay platelets and effective diffusion of surfactant molecules into layered silicate (Zawrah et al.  2014 ). Therefore, at specified surfactant levels, organomodification process was successfully carried out, and layer gaps of modified Mt considerably increased. For alkylammonium cationic surfactants, organoclay is obtained by intercalation of surfactant molecules through ion exchange with inorganic cations located in interlayer regions of clay. This process changes characteristics of Mt clay from hydrophilic to hydrophobic (Guégan  2019 ). The alkylammonium ions can form different interlamellar arrangements, which are monolayer, bilayers, pseudo‐trilayers, and paraffin‐type layer configurations, depending on the concentration of cationic surfactant, which affects basal spacing. Monolayer configuration has 13.6 Å (1.36 nm) typical basal spacing, and surfactant chains are arranged parallel to silicate layers. For bilayer structure, basal spacing is 17.6 Å, and two alkyl chains are arranged parallel to silicate layers. In pseudo‐trilayer arrangement, polar end groups of surfactant chains attach to silicate layers. Therefore, unpolar end groups of alkylammonium ions are shifted one above the other, and the thickness of three alkyl chains determines interlayer separation, yielding basal spacing of approximately 22 Å. For paraffin‐type layers, chains in all trans conformation point away from surface, whereas ammonium groups remain bonded to silicate layer, and basal spacing increases (>22 Å) depending on the number of various methyl end group orientations (Zawrah et al.  2014 ). Karaca et al. ( 2013 ) investigated the zeta potential of organoclays obtained by adding different amounts of CTAB surfactant to Mt. Negative zeta potential value of unmodified Mt increased to positive values with CTAB surfactant, which was explained by the orientation change of CTA +  ions in the basal space of clay layers from horizontal (monolayer or bilayers) to vertical positions (pseudo‐trilayers or paraffin‐type layers) (Karaca et al.  2013 ). In our study, 5‐CTAB‐oMt organoclay exhibited a zeta potential of +30.5 mV, which corresponded to basal spacing characteristic of pseudo‐trilayer structure (<22 Å), indicating successful intercalation of cationic surfactant between clay layers. The adsorption of amphiphilic surfactants in Mt clay differs from electrostatic interactions or ion exchange exhibited by cationic surfactants. The main force for adsorption between clay and non‐ionic surfactant is ion–dipole interactions. In the absence of positive charge and hydrogen bonds in interlayers for non‐ionic surfactants, ion–dipole interactions primarily control adsorption. This ensures that exchangeable inorganic cations are preserved after adsorption in clay structure, which provides both hydrophobic and hydrophilic behavior of organoclay. In general, non‐ionic surfactants adsorb on clay surfaces as lateral monolayer or bilayer structures, with interlayer spacing limited to 1.2–1.8 nm (12–18 Å) (Guégan  2019 ). Kang and Jeong ( 2015 ) studied the sorption of non‐ionic surfactant Tween80 by soil minerals. They investigated XRD patterns of Mt clay that had reacted with Tween80 surfactant. The  d ‐spacing of non‐ionic surfactant‐modified Mt clay increased to 16.5–18.9 from 12.6 Å, which was associated with the basal spacing of unmodified Mt. The  d 
 001  value of Mt increased with the addition of Tween80, indicating that absorption of Tween80 between layers results in expansion. In our study,  d ‐spacing value (16.1 Å) obtained for 3‐Tween‐oMt organoclay was consistent with the literature. The results showed that lateral bilayer structure was obtained in non‐ionic surfactant‐modified organoclay.

The addition of surfactant resulted in a substantial decrease in interfacial tension of emulsion, showing the synergy between Mt clay and surfactant. The use of surfactants altered wetting properties, caused particle size flocculation, and enhanced suspension stability. The surfactant adsorbed at particle interface on the surface of droplets, thereby decreasing interfacial tension and resulting in smaller particle sizes. Delamination of Mt clay is characterized by reduction in particle size and increase in specific surface area. The extent of delamination is influenced by the swelling capacity of clay (Mahmoodi et al.  2019 ). Mahmoodi et al. ( 2019 ) investigated the adsorption behavior of cationic surfactants onto Mt. As cationic surfactant concentration increased, the particle size of Mt increased, explained by the intercalation of positive tails of cationic surfactants in the internal layers of Mt for this phenomenon. Because of the complexity of colloidal systems, aggregation phenomena can be challenging. Brownian motion, which is random movement of particles inside suspension, causes colloidal particles to undergo unstable movement as a result of collisions with molecules of solvent and particles. This kinetic behavior can cause particle collisions followed by aggregation, thereby complicating precise regulation of cluster dimensions. Electrostatic interactions can also be another critical factor in colloidal systems, capable of triggering interactions that facilitate particle aggregation. It can be challenging to control these interactions, particularly in complex solutions, where they are modulated by factors such as particle dimensions, morphology of particles, ionic strength, dynamic interactions, and pH. Additionally, colloidal particles are influenced by van der Waals interactions in solution (Rodriguez‐Loya et al.  2024 ). When surfactant is included, adsorption of surfactant molecules onto clay interlayers may change zeta potential, increase electrostatic repulsion between platelets, and consequently lead to particle size reduction. This situation affects both van der Waals interactions and electrostatic repulsion. As surfactant concentration continues to increase, adsorption of surfactant molecules finally reaches a saturation point. Excess surfactant may then cause hydrophobic interactions, leading to micelle formation, which can cause an increase in particle size despite zeta potential remaining positive/negative (Mahmoodi et al.  2019 ; Moslemizadeh et al.  2016 ; Rodriguez‐Loya et al.  2024 ). Nanoemulsion systems are thermodynamically unstable and characterized by particle sizes typically smaller than 500 nm. The size of the particles in nanoemulsion is significantly influenced by the amount of surfactant added (Yang et al.  2020 ). In the evaluation of the type and amount of surfactant in Mt clay, it will be important to assess characterization analyses collectively and in conjunction with other characterization methods. On the basis of data presented in Table  2 , the delamination and swelling of organoclay solutions below 6‐CTAB‐oMt (361.3 nm) and 3‐Tween‐oMt (425.5 nm) levels were considered to be the factors contributing to low average particle size (<500 nm) within the aqueous phase of applied surfactants. The obtained organoclays had good suspension stability and slow agglomeration in aqueous colloidal media up to 6‐CTAB‐oMt level for cationic surfactant and 3‐Tween‐oMt level for non‐ionic surfactant, both of which had low average particle size (<500 nm) (Törnük  2014 ; Yang et al.  2020 ).

3.1.2 Zeta Potential As shown in Figure  3 , the zeta potential value of blank clay (Mt) was measured as negative (−27.0 mV), which was consistent with the negatively charged surface of Mt (Karaca et al.  2013 ). With increasing concentrations of cationic surfactant, negative zeta potential values gradually decreased and approached zero, after that shifting to positive values (ranging from +11.9 to +38.5 mV). This trend can be explained by the screening effect on electrical charges of Mt surface and electrostatic interactions, which led to a decrease in the magnitude of zeta potential. This change occurred due to electrostatic interactions between positive ions (CTA + ) in surfactant and negative regions on the surface of Mt (Güngör et al.  2001 ). Transition of zeta potential values from negative to positive signified a shift in the orientation of positive ions from parallel structure (monolayer or bilayers) to perpendicular arrangement (pseudo‐trilayers or paraffin‐type layers) at interface (Karaca et al.  2013 ). The magnitude of zeta potential serves as an indicator of potential stability of a colloidal system. When all particles in a suspension exhibit notably high negative/positive zeta potential, they tend to repel each other, thereby minimizing the possibility of flocculation. In contrast, if particles have low values of zeta potential, there is insufficient force to prevent them from flocculating/aggregating. The threshold that typically distinguishes stable from unstable suspensions is set at approximately ±30 mV. The particles with zeta potential falling below −30 mV and exceeding +30 mV are generally regarded as stable (Malvern  2013 ). In our study, the stability was obtained at 5‐CTAB‐oMt and higher concentrations of CTAB surfactant, based on zeta potential, indicating that nanoparticles were quite stable. One of the primary factors influencing zeta potential is pH (Malvern  2013 ). Because the surface charge of nanoparticles depends on the pH of the solution, zeta potential changes with the pH value of the medium in which particles are located (Ateş  2018 ). In this study, the pH of solutions was similar and close to neutral (7.710 ± 0.133). As shown in Figure  4 , the zeta potential value of organoclay decreased from −27.0 to −21.0 mV as a result of the addition of non‐ionic surfactant. This reduction suggests that non‐ionic Tween80 might have caused a less stable structure. The decreased surface potential may indicate weaker repulsion between colloidal particles and higher aggregation kinetics (Törnük  2014 ). It can be said that among the tested concentrations, 3‐Tween‐oMt level (−23.5 mV) was the closest to −30 mV stability threshold. The decreasing behavior of zeta potential in non‐ionic surfactant‐modified Mt dispersions, compared to blank dispersion, was likely resulting from the relocation of ionic species at oil/water boundary. As indicated in the study by Roldan‐Cruz et al. ( 2016 ), the characteristics of surface charges at water–oil interface are not unclear. The interfacial charge can result from the imbalance of ions present at the surface, which are produced by hydroxide (OH − ) and hydrogen (H + ) ions in water molecules. Moreover, the ions generated by dissolved carbon dioxide (CO 3 
 2−  and HCO 3

The adsorption of non‐ionic surfactant molecules may cause relocation of ionic species from interface, thus suppressing interface charge and reducing zeta potential. FT‐IR serves as an effective method for analyzing functional groups (Mahesh et al.  2011 ). With the addition of ionic and non‐ionic surfactants to clay, the appearance of asymmetric methylene (CH 2 ) stretching, symmetric CH 2  stretching, and CH 2  bending vibration peaks showed that alkyl groups of surfactants were located in clay interlayers. When cationic surfactant content in organoclay increased, new bands were observed in the range of 2927–2918, 2855–2849, 1488–1486, and 792–786 cm −1 , which related to vibrations of asymmetric CH 2  stretching, symmetric CH 2  stretching, CH 2  scissoring bending, and CH 2  rocking bending, respectively. Typically, the intensity of these new peaks increased with higher surfactant concentrations, suggesting that a greater amount of surfactant is intercalating into clay (Chanra et al.  2019 ). Kung and Hayes ( 1993 ) also pointed out that relative shifts in vibrational modes of CH 2  can be used in the evaluation of hydrophobic properties of surfactant added. Accordingly, lower frequency (energy) values reflect a more hydrophobic structure. The results obtained in this work showed that the degree of hydrophobic properties could increase with higher surfactant loading. In Table  5 , the wavelengths (energies) of CH 2  asymmetric stretching, symmetric stretching, and bending (scissoring and rocking) vibration peaks decreased with an increase in the concentration of cationic surfactant that adsorbed on clay. At relatively high surfactant levels, most of the hydration cations were surrounded by surfactant cations, which reduced the amount of water to be adsorbed, causing surface properties to change from hydrophilic to hydrophobic (Karaca et al.  2013 ). When cationic surfactant was intercalated into clay interfacial galleries, changes were also observed in Si─O─Si stretching and bending vibrations within the tetrahedral structure. Si─O─Si stretching vibration was detected at 987 cm −1  for unmodified Mt and increased to 996 cm −1  with CTAB addition, then decreased to 991 cm −1  with further surfactant increase. Si─O─Si bending vibration band was observed at 415 cm −1  for unmodified Mt and increased to 431 cm −1  with the addition of surfactant. Accordingly, the change in Si─O─Si stretching band indicated interaction between surfactant molecules and siloxane (Si─O) clay surface. The change in Si─O vibration band proved that interaction/bonding between the surfactant and silicate surface increased (Xi et al.  2005 ). Generally, it was determined that after the levels of 4‐CTAB‐oMt and 5‐CTAB‐oMt, wavelengths of absorption bands either remained the same or decreased. The FT‐IR spectrum of Mt treated with different concentrations of non‐ionic Tween80 surfactant showed intense absorption peaks of functional groups in the structure. With the increase of Tween80 concentration, new bands were observed in the range of 2930–2925, 2855–2852, 1463–1460, and 791–787 cm −1 , which correspond to vibrations of asymmetric CH 2  stretching, symmetric CH 2  stretching, CH 2  scissoring bending, and CH 2  rocking bending, respectively. These new peaks were more pronounced, especially in 3‐Tween‐oMt and 4‐Tween‐oMt spectra. It was also expected that C═O stretching vibration peak, belonging to ester group, would appear in the range of 1735–1725 cm −1  (Kura et al.  2014 ). Although C═O vibration band was absent in 1‐Tween‐oMt and 2‐Tween‐oMt, it appeared at 1725 and 1732 cm −1  in 3‐Tween‐oMt and 4‐Tween‐oMt, respectively, with increased surfactant concentration. The absence of peak for C═O bond below 3‐Tween‐oMt level might indicate that non‐ionic surfactant was not totally adsorbed on the surface of clay at lower surfactant levels. The reason for that Tween80, which has non‐ionic structure and cannot ionize, may have caused difficulty for the surfactant molecules to adsorb on clay surface (Liu et al.  2018 ).

3.1.5 XRD Analysis According to the characterization analyses mentioned above, 5‐CTAB‐oMt and 3‐Tween‐oMt organoclays generally gave the best results. For these organoclays and unmodified Mt, the degree of intercalation and exfoliation was assessed through XRD analysis. By using Bragg's Law, the interlayer spacing ( d ‐spacing), in relation to 2 θ , was calculated and illustrated in Figure  8 . XRD curve in Figure  8a  shows the diffraction peak of unmodified Mt corresponding to  d 
 001  distance at 6.2° (2 θ ). The diffraction peaks of the organoclays of cationic surfactant modified (5‐CTAB‐oMt) and non‐ionic surfactant modified (3‐Tween‐oMt) shifted to 4.1° and 5.5°, respectively. The shift to lower values in the diffraction peak of organoclays gave strong evidence that the formation of intercalation/exfoliation was obtained (Zawrah et al.  2014 ). The layer spacing for unmodified Mt clay, 3‐Tween‐oMt, and 5‐CTAB‐oMt were calculated to be 1.43, 1.61, and 2.15 nm, respectively. XRD analysis proved that layer spacing of modified Mt clay with surfactants increased significantly, achieving successful preparation of organoclays. In the literature, when investigating XRD patterns of Mt clay, it can be seen that 2 θ  value is generally examined up to 10°. For example, Essawy et al. ( 2014 ) investigated Mt clays with different levels of CTAB surfactant between 2 θ  values of 2° and 10° for intercalation. In the work by Kang and Jeong ( 2015 ), the sorption mechanisms of Tween80 surfactant by Mt were investigated, and XRD patterns of organoclays with different surfactant concentrations were analyzed between 2° and 10° in 2 θ . The data presented in the literature were coherent with our study. Basal reflection  d ‐spacing of unmodified Mt was obtained as 1.43 nm, falling within 1.2–1.6 nm range of smectite clays under ambient conditions (Chanra et al.  2019 ). Bai et al. ( 2020 ) obtained an XRD pattern of pure Mt clay (Na–Mt) that gave a peak at 7.1°, and as a result of organomodification process with CTAB surfactant, diffraction peak shifted to 4.1°. They calculated the layer spacing as 1.24 nm for Na–Mt and 2.15 nm for oMt. In our study, the increase in  d ‐spacing and the decrease in 2 θ  value showed separation between clay platelets and effective diffusion of surfactant molecules into layered silicate (Zawrah et al.  2014 ). Therefore, at specified surfactant levels, organomodification process was successfully carried out, and layer gaps of modified Mt considerably increased. For alkylammonium cationic surfactants, organoclay is obtained by intercalation of surfactant molecules through ion exchange with inorganic cations located in interlayer regions of clay. This process changes characteristics of Mt clay from hydrophilic to hydrophobic (Guégan  2019 ). The alkylammonium ions can form different interlamellar arrangements, which are monolayer, bilayers, pseudo‐trilayers, and paraffin‐type layer configurations, depending on the concentration of cationic surfactant, which affects basal spacing. Monolayer configuration has 13.6 Å (1.36 nm) typical basal spacing, and surfactant chains are arranged parallel to silicate layers. For bilayer structure, basal spacing is 17.6 Å, and two alkyl chains are arranged parallel to silicate layers. In pseudo‐trilayer arrangement, polar end groups of surfactant chains attach to silicate layers. Therefore, unpolar end groups of alkylammonium ions are shifted one above the other, and the thickness of three alkyl chains determines interlayer separation, yielding basal spacing of approximately 22 Å. For paraffin‐type layers, chains in all trans conformation point away from surface, whereas ammonium groups remain bonded to silicate layer, and basal spacing increases (>22 Å) depending on the number of various methyl end group orientations (Zawrah et al.  2014 ). Karaca et al. ( 2013 ) investigated the zeta potential of organoclays obtained by adding different amounts of CTAB surfactant to Mt. Negative zeta potential value of unmodified Mt increased to positive values with CTAB surfactant, which was explained by the orientation change of CTA +  ions in the basal space of clay layers from horizontal (monolayer or bilayers) to vertical positions (pseudo‐trilayers or paraffin‐type layers) (Karaca et al.  2013 ). In our study, 5‐CTAB‐oMt organoclay exhibited a zeta potential of +30.5 mV, which corresponded to basal spacing characteristic of pseudo‐trilayer structure (<22 Å), indicating successful intercalation of cationic surfactant between clay layers. The adsorption of amphiphilic surfactants in Mt clay differs from electrostatic interactions or ion exchange exhibited by cationic surfactants. The main force for adsorption between clay and non‐ionic surfactant is ion–dipole interactions. In the absence of positive charge and hydrogen bonds in interlayers for non‐ionic surfactants, ion–dipole interactions primarily control adsorption. This ensures that exchangeable inorganic cations are preserved after adsorption in clay structure, which provides both hydrophobic and hydrophilic behavior of organoclay. In general, non‐ionic surfactants adsorb on clay surfaces as lateral monolayer or bilayer structures, with interlayer spacing limited to 1.2–1.8 nm (12–18 Å) (Guégan  2019 ). Kang and Jeong ( 2015 ) studied the sorption of non‐ionic surfactant Tween80 by soil minerals. They investigated XRD patterns of Mt clay that had reacted with Tween80 surfactant. The  d ‐spacing of non‐ionic surfactant‐modified Mt clay increased to 16.5–18.9 from 12.6 Å, which was associated with the basal spacing of unmodified Mt. The  d 
 001  value of Mt increased with the addition of Tween80, indicating that absorption of Tween80 between layers results in expansion. In our study,  d ‐spacing value (16.1 Å) obtained for 3‐Tween‐oMt organoclay was consistent with the literature. The results showed that lateral bilayer structure was obtained in non‐ionic surfactant‐modified organoclay.

The addition of unmodified/modified clay in biopolymer structure notably reduced water absorption when compared to control film (S). In general, incorporation of clay/organoclay resulted in a reduction in  W A 
  ranging from 31.5% to 42.3%. This reduction could be attributed to interactions between polymer and nanoparticles. As a result, free water molecules exhibited weaker interactions with nanocomposite films (Sadegh‐Hassani and Mohammadi Nafchi  2014 ). When comparing the samples, it was observed that nanocomposites with unmodified clays (S‐Mt) exhibited higher water absorption values than those containing organoclays. Overall, increasing nanofiller concentration to 3% resulted in a drastic decrease in water absorption capacity. In the literature, similar findings were reported, indicating a reduction in water absorption capacity of nanocomposites containing clays compared to control material. Cyras et al. ( 2008 ) investigated diffusion of water in starch/Mt nanocomposite films and showed that water absorption capacity decreased with incorporation of nanoclay. They suggested that this reduction could be attributed to the formation of hydrogen bonds between matrix and hydroxyl groups in silicate layers, as well as tortuous paths created by nanoclays. These structural modifications could hinder diffusion of water molecules in the nanocomposite structure, thereby reducing water absorption capacity. Pandey and Singh ( 2005 ) evaluated water uptake properties of Mt‐added TPS over a period of time. They reported that control film exhibited the highest moisture sensitivity compared to nanocomposites. After the addition of nanoclay, the hydrophilicity of materials decreased significantly. It was also noted that superior dispersion of nanofillers in polymer likely led to greater interaction between hydroxyl groups and silicate layers, thereby reducing their availability for water absorption. They also identified two additional molecular forces in matrix, polymer‐plasticizer, and clay‐plasticizer, which affected water absorption capacity. The dispersion level of nanoclay platelets had a more significant impact on altering the water sensitivity of the material than the presence of moisture‐sensitive groups like plasticizer. Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ) prepared starch/polyvinyl alcohol/glycerol matrix (ST/PVA/GL) containing varying concentrations of halloysite nanotube (HNT) and obtained a significant decrease in water absorption capacity with increasing nanoparticle concentration. However, after reaching a certain threshold of clay level, further increases in clay concentration resulted in either nearly constant or minimal reduction in water absorption capacity, which was also noted in our study. They attributed this phenomenon to clumping of nanoclay in matrix. In our study, increasing organoclay content from 3% to 5% resulted in a slight reduction for water absorption. However, the absence of a statistically significant difference could be attributed to the heterogenous distribution of nanofiller and agglomeration occurring at higher concentrations. In water solubility, increasing clay/organoclay content in matrix to 3% significantly decreased the results. The control film (S) exhibited the highest water solubility, which can be attributed to partial miscibility of components, with a substantial number of free hydroxyl groups being available to interact with water molecules (Abdullah and Dong  2019 ). As a result, the addition of clay/organoclay into biopolymer reduced  W S 
  values by approximately 41.0%–50.1%. At 3% level, nanocomposites containing modified organoclay (S‐CTAB‐oMt‐3%, S‐Tween‐oMt‐3%) demonstrated lower water solubility compared to samples containing unmodified clay (S‐Mt‐3%). This result indicated that surfactants assisted in intercalation or exfoliation of nanoparticles at this level, resulting in more homogeneous nanocomposite structures (Mahesh et al.  2011 ). Statistically, nanocomposites with 3% organoclay generally exhibited the lowest water solubility. Hydrophobicity of starch‐based nanocomposites was obtained by adding clay nanofillers into matrix, which obtained replacing hydroxyl groups with hydrophobic functional groups (Agarwal  2021 ). Most biopolymers are highly sensitive to water, and their water solubility can play a critical role in determining potential applications of biopolymer composites (Sadegh‐Hassani and Mohammadi Nafchi  2014 ). As water molecules penetrate the matrix, the size of biopolymer may change, and extractable components may be removed (Cyras et al.  2008 ). Incorporation of an appropriate concentration of clay nanoparticles in structure can reduce the amount of soluble matter lost during immersion in water (Abdullah and Dong  2019 ). Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ) and Tunç and Duman ( 2010 ) similarly reported that adding clay nanofillers reduced water solubility by inhibiting water diffusion into nanocomposite matrix. In our study, increasing organoclay content from 3% to 5% resulted in either the same or slightly increased water solubility. This trend was particularly pronounced for the materials prepared with organoclays containing cationic surfactants. This situation can be attributed to nanoparticle agglomeration and a consequent decrease in water resistance, as also indicated by water absorption capacity results (Abdullah and Dong  2019 ). 3.2.2 Migration Analyses Food contact materials and articles, including bio‐based and/or biodegradable ones, must comply with the standards established by the Framework Regulation (EC) 1935/2004 (European Commission  2004 ). Bio‐based plastics are regulated under Regulation (EU) 10/2011 issued by the EU (Union  2025 ). The regulated testing conditions established for traditional fossil‐based plastics are anticipated to be suitable for bio‐based/biodegradable plastic materials as well. Therefore, it is important to assess the compliance of bio‐based materials produced for food contact according to relevant regulations (Lestido‐Cardama et al.  2025 ). The main purpose for examining migration characteristics of food packaging materials is to assess potential adverse health effects that may arise from exposure to harmful components. Food simulants are used to determine the extent of migration that may occur into various types of foods. Migration tests are designed to simplify experimental procedures and simulate real‐world conditions under anticipated test conditions (de Abreu et al.  2010 ). 3.2.2.1 Overall Migration Analysis Analysis results are given in Table  7  and illustrated in Figure  10 . Film samples containing 3% organoclay statistically had the lowest migration results for both simulants, remained below overall migration limit (OML: 10 mg/dm 2 ), and represented optimal performance in terms of minimizing overall migration. However, increasing organoclay content from 3% to 5% led to higher migration results, which generally exceeded OML allowed by legislation, except for S‐Tween‐oMt‐5% sample in hydrophilic simulant. The highest overall migration results were obtained for acidic simulant. Overall migration analysis is conducted to determine the mass of non‐volatile substances that can migrate from plastic sample into foodstuff/food simulants (European Committee for Standardization  2022 ). According to legislation outlined in the EU and Türkiye (Union  2025 ; Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry  2024 ), overall migration from plastic materials and articles into food/food simulants must not exceed 10 mg for each dm 2  of surface in contact with food. Literature shows that adding nanoclay up to a certain level in materials can reduce total migration, as found in this work. In the study undertaken by Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ), the production of biodegradable nanocomposite films was obtained by incorporating varying concentrations (0.25%–0.50%–1%–3%–5% w/w) of HNT nanoclay into ST/PVA/GL matrix. They investigated overall migration rates in 10% ethanol (simulant A) and 3% acetic acid (simulant B) at 40°C for 10 days. The films containing 1% and 3% nanoclay exhibited migration values below OML in simulant A. Hydrophilic structure of films could enhance their solubility in a hydrophilic simulant. The addition of hydrophobic HNT nanofiller contributed to a reduction in total migration and reduced solubility of nanocomposites. Furthermore, the formation of interfacial bonds between polymer matrix and nanoclay limited mass transfer into simulant. However, it was stated that 5% HNT might have led to nanoparticle agglomeration, thereby increasing total migration rate. In our study, for hydrophilic simulant, all film materials containing 3% clay/organoclay exhibited total migration values below the regulatory limit. As reported in the literature, our results similarly showed that increasing the amount of clay/organoclay from 3% to 5% in bio‐based material resulted in higher total migration values due to agglomeration, which caused it to exceed OML. Echegoyen et al. ( 2016 ) examined Mt nanoclay in commercial low‐density polyethylene, using hydrophilic and acidic simulants, and investigated specific migration of aluminum ions. Specific migration results obtained with the hydrophilic simulant were four to five times lower than those obtained with the acidic one. This was attributed to an increased ion release rate as pH decreased. In a similar manner, our work showed that films in acidic simulant had higher overall migration values than 10% ethanol. Cano et al. ( 2015 ) carried out overall migration tests on films composed of pea starch/polyvinyl alcohol and cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) at different concentrations (1%–3%–5%), using simulants of isooctane and 10% ethanol. Isooctane simulant was used to mimic fatty (non‐polar) foodstuffs, whereas 10% ethanol represented polar foodstuffs. They reported that there was no significant difference ( p  < 0.05) in migration values between control and nanocomposite films for 10% ethanol, except for the ones containing 5% CNC, which exhibited higher migration; all migration results remained below OML. In a similar manner, our study also demonstrated a rising trend of total migration values with increasing amounts of clay/organoclay, from 3% to 5%. In the study by Cano et al. ( 2015 ), the highest migration result in isooctane simulant was obtained for control film, although the values were approximately 100 times lower than those in 10% ethanol. The addition of CNC into the structure resulted in a nearly fourfold reduction in migration levels in isooctane. The distinct migration behavior of control and CNC‐containing materials in these simulants was interpreted as having hydrophilic polar nature of CNC. As a result, the addition of CNC to film composition effectively reduced overall migration into hydrophobic, non‐polar isooctane. Similarly, Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ) reported that overall migration rates were lowest in food simulant B compared to simulant A. Nevertheless, our study demonstrated that elevated overall migration results were obtained for the samples tested with 3% acetic acid compared to 10% ethanol. The regulations specify that 3% acetic acid is also assigned for foodstuffs that have hydrophilic character, similar to 10% ethanol (Union  2025 ; Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry  2024 ). In the study, it was evident that the decrease in hydrophilic structure of starch with the addition of a 3% level of hydrophobic clay/organoclay to matrix resulted in decrease in total migration for both acidic and hydrophilic simulants. According to the Council of Europe ( 1992 ), the most vigorous food simulant is stated as 3% acetic acid, and metal migration tests should be implemented only in acidic simulant. This highlights the importance of specific migration analyses. Mt is an alumina‐silicate clay mineral that can contain metal oxides in its structure (Chai et al.  2024 ). In our study, during overall migration analysis with 3% acetic acid, metal ions could migrate from film material into acidic simulant, which could potentially explain increase in overall migration results exceeding OML. 3.2.2.2 Specific Migration Analysis On the basis of ICP analysis, hydrophilic simulant exhibited the weakest interaction with nanocomposites, which was consistent with overall migration analysis. Similarly, Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ) reported that overall migration rates were lowest in food simulant B compared to simulant A. Nevertheless, our study demonstrated that elevated overall migration results were obtained for the samples tested with 3% acetic acid compared to 10% ethanol. The regulations specify that 3% acetic acid is also assigned for foodstuffs that have hydrophilic character, similar to 10% ethanol (Union  2025 ; Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry  2024 ). In the study, it was evident that the decrease in hydrophilic structure of starch with the addition of a 3% level of hydrophobic clay/organoclay to matrix resulted in decrease in total migration for both acidic and hydrophilic simulants. According to the Council of Europe ( 1992 ), the most vigorous food simulant is stated as 3% acetic acid, and metal migration tests should be implemented only in acidic simulant. This highlights the importance of specific migration analyses. Mt is an alumina‐silicate clay mineral that can contain metal oxides in its structure (Chai et al.  2024 ). In our study, during overall migration analysis with 3% acetic acid, metal ions could migrate from film material into acidic simulant, which could potentially explain increase in overall migration results exceeding OML.

Likewise, overall migration analysis showed that the results obtained with acidic simulant were higher than those obtained with the aqueous one. The results conducted with acidic simulant showed statistically significant differences ( p  < 0.05) for all materials (Figure  11 ). This indicates that the type of surfactant (cationic/non‐ionic) and level of organoclay used are important in specific migration behavior with acidic simulant. In all samples, specific migration levels of aluminum were significantly lower than the regulation limit (1 mg/kg), as stipulated by the EU and Turkish food contact materials legislations (Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry  2024 ; Union  2025 ).
