Relevant studies in the literature, as demonstrated in the present study, indicate that incorporating nanoclay into material leads to specific migration of aluminum. In the study conducted by Farhoodi et al. ( 2014 ), nanocomposite samples were prepared by blending commercial organoclay into polyethylene terephthalate matrix. Total immersion method using 3% acetic acid was employed to evaluate specific migration of Al element at 25°C and 45°C for 7–90 days. The portions of simulants were taken at time intervals, and aluminum concentration was analyzed. The results indicated that specific migration of Al increased with prolonged storage time and higher temperature. At 25°C, aluminum levels rose from 0.03 mg/kg on Day 10 to 0.18 mg/kg on Day 90, whereas at 45°C, migration increased from 0.06 to 0.34 mg/kg over the same period. Specific migration results obtained in our study using acidic simulant were generally lower compared to the findings reported by Farhoodi et al. ( 2014 ). Although the main polymer matrices examined in two studies differ, this discrepancy may be attributed to the shorter contact time employed in our study. Mauricio‐Iglesias et al. ( 2010 ) incorporated Mt into wheat gluten matrix to develop food contact materials and investigated migration properties in water, 3% acetic acid, and 15% ethanol simulants after 10 days of storage at 40°C. Their results indicated that significant amounts of Al migration were detected only in acidic simulant, as observed in our study. This was attributed to the greater solubility of Al under low pH conditions, as Mt can undergo ion exchange within its interlayer regions. In the presence of acetic acid, an abundance of hydrogen ions may have replaced some of interlayer aluminum ions, which could explain aluminum migration. As stated by Council of Europe ( 1992 ), 3% acetic acid is regarded as the most aggressive simulant in terms of metal migration for plastics. Abdullah and Dong ( 2019 ) investigated specific migration of Al ions from halloysite nanoclay combined into developed ST/PVA/GL biomaterial at 40°C for 10 days, using acidic and aqueous simulants. Aluminum ions were detected in both simulants; however, in contrast to the findings of our study, they reported higher migration levels in the aqueous simulant compared to the acidic one. This outcome was attributed to the hydrophilic character of 10% ethanol, which exhibited a solvent‐like effect on nanocomposites similar to that of water. This interaction enhanced the mobility of polymer chains, thereby facilitating the release of nanoclay from matrix. Additionally, it was reported that increasing HNT content in matrix led to a rise in Al migration for both simulants. In our study, a similar trend was observed by increasing the cationic surfactant‐modified organoclay ratio from 3% to 5% in matrix. This phenomenon was attributed to the formation of nanoclay agglomerates at higher nanoparticle concentrations, leading to poor interfacial bonding and greater migration into acidic simulant compared to well‐dispersed nanoparticles embedded in polymer matrix (Abdullah and Dong  2019 ). In food simulants, two mechanisms influence the mass transfer of nanoparticles: embedding (intermolecular interactions between polymer chains and penetrants) and diffusion, known as dual sorption theory. Among these, the diffusion proceeds at a faster rate than the embedding mechanism. Acetic acid and water molecules first embed in the matrix, then act as plasticizers, expanding polymer chains. This expansion causes the migration of nanoparticles through the equilibrated matrix (Farhoodi et al.  2014 ; Abdullah and Dong  2019 ; Huang et al.  2011 ). However, the primary advantage of incorporating nanoclay lies in its ability to significantly increase barrier properties of material against the permeation of gases or liquids (penetrants). The most widely accepted explanation for the improvement in barrier properties is provided by Nielsen's theory (Nielsen  1967 ). According to this theory, when nanofillers like clay in matrix are impermeable to liquid or gas molecules, these penetrant molecules are forced to navigate around fillers, resulting in a tortuous diffusion path (Mahesh et al.  2011 ; Törnük  2014 ). This increased diffusion path length effectively prolongs migration route and improves the barrier efficiency of the material. Due to the relatively rapid nature of the diffusion mechanism compared to the slower embedding process, diffusion of acetic acid molecules into starch‐based nanocomposites contributed to expansion between polymeric chains and promoted release of clay/organoclay. Therefore, it can be stated that in our study, the diffusion mechanism played a dominant role in controlling specific migration rates, which were higher in acidic simulant compared to hydrophilic counterparts.

4 Conclusion Clay‐based nanocomposite materials play a significant role in the development of novel and innovative food packaging materials. One of the primary concerns regarding the use of nanocomposites in food packaging is their safety, which significantly restricts their broader application and acceptance. The risks associated with these nanomaterials remain largely undefined due to a lack of comprehensive research. In the present study, special attention was given to ensuring that selected clay and surfactants were among those permitted for use in the production of food contact substances and materials, in accordance with the legislations of the EU and Türkiye. These regulations support commercial development of packaging films while ensuring the safety of materials and their potential impact on food products. The incorporation of studied organoclays into starch, a promising biopolymer, for the development of active food packaging films was an effective approach, considering the results in terms of water absorption capacity, water solubility, and migration analyses. In this study, the adsorption behavior of cationic and non‐ionic surfactants onto the layers of Mt clay was investigated using various characterization methods, including particle size analysis, zeta potential, electrical conductivity, FT‐IR, and XRD measurements to assess the effects of surfactant type and surfactant/clay ratio. Particle size analysis showed that organoclays exhibited good suspension stability and slow agglomeration in aqueous colloidal media up to 6‐CTAB‐oMt level for cationic surfactant and 3‐Tween‐oMt level for non‐ionic surfactant. Meanwhile, zeta potential measurement indicated that stable suspensions (>+30 mV) were obtained for 5‐CTAB‐oMt and higher cationic surfactant levels, while among organoclays containing non‐ionic surfactants, 3‐Tween‐oMt showed the best zeta potential, closest to −30 mV stability threshold. Besides, the electrical conductivity and surfactant concentration graph for cationic surfactant showed a decrease in conductivity at 5‐CTAB‐oMt level, where the graph deviated from linearity. As conductivity depends on ion concentration in solution, no consistent increase was observed with increasing non‐ionic surfactant levels due to its electrically neutral hydrophilic head. In FT‐IR measurements, the wavelengths of absorption bands either remained constant or decreased after 4‐CTAB‐oMt or 5‐CTAB‐oMt levels for cationic surfactant. In the case of non‐ionic surfactant, energies of vibration peaks increased up to 3‐Tween‐oMt level, after which they remained unchanged or decreased. Additionally, absorption band corresponding to oxygen‐containing functional group in surfactant was first detected at 3‐Tween‐oMt level. As a result, the synthesis of organoclays was successful at 5‐CTAB‐oMt and 3‐Tween‐oMt levels. XRD patterns showed dispersion morphology and interlayer spacing of oMt, providing insights into spatial orientation of surfactant molecules within basal regions. The selected levels of cationic (5‐CTAB‐oMt) and non‐ionic (3‐Tween‐oMt) surfactants were successfully intercalated and exfoliated Mt platelets. Mt nanofillers created a tortuous structure, reducing free space available for water uptake within the material. When organoclays were uniformly dispersed throughout polymer, they effectively helped to block water penetration. These findings were further supported by reduction in the hydrophilic nature of films upon incorporation of organoclays, as reflected in a decrease in overall migration results for both acidic and hydrophilic simulants. The interfacial bonds between organoclay nanofiller and starch matrix strengthened the structure, thereby reducing solubility and limiting mass transfer into both food simulants. Notably, a 3% level of organoclay in the films significantly lowered overall migration results below the regulation limit (10 mg/dm 2 ), meeting strict food safety requirements. Specific migration analysis showed that organoclay particles were capable of migrating from starch‐based nanocomposites into acidic simulant but remained well below (84.3%–96.4%) the 1 mg/kg regulatory limit for aluminum. Al element was not detected (<LOQ) in aqueous simulant under test conditions. Intercalation, driven by increased interactions between organoclay surface and polymer chains, likely reduced migration values into both simulants by restricting mobility of polymer chains and organoclay layers at polymer–clay interface. Moreover, excessive incorporation of organoclay in matrix led to agglomeration, resulting in increased overall and specific migration values. It is therefore essential to accurately determine the optimum amount of organoclay to be used in biopolymer. The improvements conferred by the obtained organoclays on migration characteristics of starch‐based nanocomposite films highlight their potential use in sustainable food packaging applications, particularly for hydrophilic and acidic foodstuffs. With the incorporation of organoclay, more hydrophobic and stable food packaging materials were successfully developed. These results thus contribute to the development of a more sustainable and environmentally friendly approach within food packaging plastics industry. In conclusion, although substantial progress has been made in recent years to ensure compliance of food contact materials with common usage scenarios, it remains essential to further develop these studies to also address more specific or emerging cases, particularly those falling within the scope of active and intelligent packaging. Nanocomposites incorporating nanoclays are already commercially available in packaging market, and their areas of application continue to expand within food packaging industry. Therefore, future studies are needed to investigate different food groups and storage conditions for organoclay‐containing food packaging materials.
